newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge formally endorses Valdez verdict.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge formally endorses Valdez verdict.

text.p: A federal judge on Tuesday entered formal judgment on the $5 billion fine slapped on Exxon Corp by a jury two years ago as punishment for the disasterous 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill.

U.S. District Court Judge H. Russel Holland approved the punitive fine -- the largest assessed by a jury against a corporation -- along with compensation to commercial fishermen, accrued interest and a $5,000 punitive fine against former Exxon supertanker captain Joseph Hazelwood.
The entry of judgment ended years of litigation at the District Court level, one plaintiff attorney said.

"This is the principle goal to which we have been striving for the last 7 1/2 years," said Dave Oesting, a lead attorney for the thousands of fishermen, Alaska Natives, property owners and others who sued the oil giant over the 11 million gallon (41.6 million litres) spill.
"We finally achieved closure at the trial court level of all aspects of this litigation," Oesting said.
The formal entry of judgment allows Exxon to appeal the trial verdict to a higher court. The company has said it intends to seek a reversal from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

Holland's order approved $19.5 million in compensation -- the result of the $287 million that the jury ordered in payment to approximately 10,000 commercial salmon and herring fishermen, minus credits for previous payments made by Exxon.
The order also assessed the pre-judgment interest at $37.9 million, billed to both Exxon and Hazelwood.
The totals result from a summer-long, three-phase trial conducted in Holland's court in 1994.

In most civil trials, formal judgment is entered shortly after juries issue their verdicts. But judgment in the Exxon Valdez case was delayed because of the complicated nature of the litigation. It involved two civil trials in federal and state courts and several separate settlements for various plaintiff groups.

The oil disaster occurred March 24, 1989, when the Exxon Valdez supertanker grounded on a reef in Prince William Sound. The tanker, under Hazelwood's command, spewed 11 million gallons (41.6 million litres) of oil into the icy waters, spreading over more 1,200 shoreline miles (1,900 km) and affecting national parks and a national forest.
It killed thousands of marine mammals and hundred of thousands of seabirds, government scientists said.

Exxon spent over $2 billion to clean up the spill. In 1991, the company agreed to pay $1.025 billion over 10 years to settle federal and state government civil and criminal complaints over environmental damages.
